That split has a name, the weak generational hypothesis.
Most objects die young.
In one real collection, the young objects were twenty-seven MB still alive and four hundred seventy MB of garbage.
HotSpot's collectors split the heap to match.
New objects go into eden, in the young generation.
Objects that stay alive end up in the old generation.
Your code fills eden with new objects, and most of them die soon after.
When eden fills, a young collection starts.
It follows references from the roots and finds the few objects that are still alive.
It copies them into an empty survivor space, and each one's age goes up by one.
Then all of eden is free at once.
The collector never even looks at the dead objects.
So a young collection costs time in proportion to what survives, not to what was allocated.
There is a catch.
Moving an object is only safe while no thread is using it.
So first, every application thread stops at a safepoint, a known place where the collector can find and fix its references.
That is a stop-the-world pause.
In G one, every young collection runs inside such a pause.
This time the live objects from eden and from the survivor space are copied to the other survivor space.
Then the threads run again.
The age lives in four bits of each object's header.
After enough survivals, at most fifteen, an object is promoted to the old generation, which is collected much less often.
This is why medium-lived objects are the expensive kind.
They get copied at every young collection, then promoted, and then they die in the old generation, where only a bigger collection can free them.
An idempotency cache with a ten-minute expiry has exactly that shape.
